key_insight: Oscillating floating planar bodies at an air-water interface experience hydrodynamic resistance that is well described by oscillatory Stokes boundary-layer theory in the high-Womersley, small-amplitude limit.
engineering_relevance: The work provides a practical way to extract effective added mass and damping for interfacial devices from frequency-response measurements, useful for designing and controlling floating sensors, actuators, and microfluidic systems.
method: Drive planar interfacial bodies harmonically with magnetic actuation
Measure steady-state amplitude response and phase lag across frequencies, masses, sizes, and shapes
Compare startup transients to a history-integral model for oscillatory boundary-layer development
evidence_signal: The abstract reports agreement between measured frequency-response behavior and oscillatory boundary-layer theory, and also shows that transient startup dynamics are accurately predicted by a history-integral model.
watch_item: The theory and extracted coefficients are stated to be valid primarily in the small-deformation, high-Womersley regime, so stronger interface deformation or lower-frequency cases may require more complex modeling.
paper_title: Hydrodynamic Resistance on Oscillating Planar Interfacial Bodies
